newsitem.title: ZAIRE: New tide of refugees said heading towards Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: New tide of refugees said heading towards Rwanda.

text.p: Hundreds of Rwandan refugees arrived in the eastern Zairean town of Goma on Tuesday and told aid workers that many more were massing around Sake, a town 20 km (12 miles) to the west, an aid worker said.
"We have had around 700 refugees coming from Sake today," said Sudi Balibwazi, a local worker for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR.
"These refugees are reporting a long column of refugees stretching back from Sake into the Masisi and can only estimate the numbers as many thousands," Balibwazi said.

The latest refugees were all from the camps around Goma but he said a small number had already come from Bukavu, to the south of Lake Kivu, and that they had said there were many more refugees behind them.
This movement could herald the return of a second wave of refugees back home to Rwanda.

Up to 600,000 are estimated to have returned since November 15 when they decided en masse to leave east Zaire to escape fighting between the Zairean army, Zairean rebels and Rwandan Hutu extremists who controlled the refugee camps.
The flood has slowed to a trickle in recent days, despite reports of large numbers of refugees heading north along the lake towards Goma or hiding in the forest to the west.
"I came from Katale camp 30 days ago," said Samson Kwinduyira, 16, a Rwandan refugee who had walked through the Masisi region arriving in Sake on Monday.
"The column of refugees stretches back into the Masisi and there is fighting in the Masisi between the rebels and the former Rwandan government army," he said.

"In the last two days we have had 1,400 refugees from Bukavu who have arrived in Sake, and come back to Rwanda via Goma, but now, perhaps because of fighting, those in Sake might have taken to the hills," said Ray Wilkinson, a spokesman for the UNHCR in Goma.

Earlier, a U.S. navy plane circled the sky above Goma and Sake in an effort to locate the refugees, with aid agencies showing frustration at their inability to help people who may have been without proper food for several weeks.
Access to Sake, 20 kms (12 miles) west of Goma, was again denied to journalists and foreign aid workers on Tuesday by rebel troops, although local cars and minibuses were allowed through.

Aid workers had to quit the Kivu area when the fighting flared up in October, and the rebels have not allowed them in since, although they agreed this week to allow assessment work to begin in the Bukavu region.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees estimated there were 1.2 million Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire until mid-November, but the number and whereabouts of those that are still there is a source of controversy.
The Rwandan government has said there are no genuine refugees left, only soldiers of the former Rwandan army and Hutu militias, plus their families.
For that reason, it maintains there is no need for a planned multinational intervention force to help the aid effort in Zaire and has refused to allow any force to be based in Rwanda.

Western and African military officials who met in Stuttgart over the weekend agreed on scenarios to help feed the refugees in Zaire but enthusiasm for the mission has waned since the refugees started flooding home.
France expressed anger at the foot-dragging on Monday.

"I am frankly shocked when I see that kind of apathy hiding behind endless discussions," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said in Brussels. "It is urgent. The French position is that the international force...is more than ever necessary."
